title: Comparing groups with a t-test
explanation: Biology sessions average 80.5 points and Economics only 66.75. But with so few sessions, could that gap just be luck? A **t-test** checks whether the difference between two group averages is bigger than you'd expect by chance. Its **p-value** answers: "if there were really no difference, how likely is a gap this big?" A p-value **under 0.05** is the usual bar for calling a difference **statistically significant**.

tasks.prompt: Keep just the Biology and Economics sessions, and store them in two_subjects.

tasks.teach: **t.test(number ~ group, data = ...)** compares the averages of exactly 2 groups. Run `test` on its own to see the full report, including both averages.
tasks.prompt: Run the t-test: test <- t.test(score ~ subject, data = two_subjects). Then store its p-value in p: p <- test$p.value.
hints: Same ~ idea as lm(): the number on the left, the 2 groups on the right.
test <- t.test(score ~ subject, data = two_subjects), then p <- test$p.value
tasks.answer:
test <- t.test(score ~ subject, data = two_subjects)
p <- test$p.value

tasks.teach: Here p is about 0.09, above 0.05, so it's **not** significant: with only 4 sessions each, a 14-point gap could plausibly be chance. That doesn't prove there's **no** difference. It means this data isn't enough to be confident. More sessions would tell us more.
tasks.prompt: Last one: is the difference significant at the usual 0.05 level? Store p < 0.05 in significant (it will be TRUE or FALSE).
hints: A comparison gives TRUE or FALSE.

recap: t.test(number ~ group) checks whether two group averages really differ. A p-value under 0.05 is the usual bar for significance, and small samples often aren't enough to be sure.
